titleText.es: Los foros de huracanes están llenos de comentarios excitados sobre la presión central y la velocidad del viento y comparaciones con Camille y 1931 y 1938, con la coletilla de rigor sobre lo trágico que sería que muriera alguien y que esperan que no sea para tanto.
titleText.en: Hurricane forums are full of excited comments about central pressure and wind speed and comparisons to Camille and 1931 and 1938, with hastily-tacked-on notes about how it will be tragic if anyone dies and they hope it's a dud.
titleText.noteEn: The English text is the official xkcd title text. The Spanish raster translates intern as residente and preserves the archive wording DISPARARLE even though its following target, SUS VENTANAS, is plural; that number mismatch is explained only at the occurrence. Vision also split ATRACCIÓN, ESPERANZAS, and ATERRORIZADOS across printed line breaks, lost the accents in HARÁN, ÓRGANOS, and SOLÍAN, and misread HUMANOS and CONVERSACIONES. This artifact follows the visible raster exactly.

regions.labelEs: ME HE DADO CUENTA DE QUE ANIMO SECRETAMENTE A LOS HURACANES. VEO LAS NOTICIAS CON LA ESPERANZA DE QUE SE HARÁN ENORMES Y ARRASARÁN UNA CIUDAD. SÉ QUE MIS ESPERANZAS NO LOS AFECTAN EN REALIDAD, PERO ME SIENTO MAL.

applications.exampleEs: ME HE DADO CUENTA DE QUE
applications.explanationEn: Me matches the speaker; he dado supplies the completed form of dar; cuenta completes the fixed expression; and de que introduces the fact noticed.
He is the present form of haber for the speaker, and dado is dar's completed-action form.
Secreta is the feminine singular form of secreto; adding -mente forms secretamente, which describes how the speaker roots for the hurricanes.
A marks the personified hurricanes as the direct target of animo, and los huracanes completes the plural target phrase.
Se with harán forms hacerse for a plural subject, and enormes names the resulting state.
Harán uses hacer's irregular future stem har- plus the plural ending -án.
Arrasarán keeps the full form arrasar and adds the plural future ending -án.
Los replaces the masculine plural things affected and stands directly before the conjugated verb afectan.
The two words form the fixed contrast marker en realidad.
Me matches the speaker, siento is the corresponding form of sentir, and mal supplies the negative feeling.

regions.labelEs: NA, NO ES MÁS QUE LA ATRACCIÓN NATURAL DE LOS HUMANOS POR EL ESPECTÁCULO. ES COMO VER EL LANZAMIENTO DE UN TRANSBORDADOR ESPACIAL PORQUE NO TE QUIERES PERDER UN POSIBLE DESASTRE.

applications.explanationEn: No makes es negative, and más que limits what follows to the sole explanation being presented.
Porque is one unaccented word because it introduces a reason here.

applications.exampleEs: TE QUIERES PERDER UN POSIBLE DESASTRE
applications.explanationEn: Te matches the listener, perder supplies the action, and desastre is the experience that would be missed; quieres sits between the marker and the unchanged verb in this two-verb structure.
Quieres changes for one familiar listener, while perder remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: O VESTIRTE COMO UN RESIDENTE PARA COLARTE EN LAS SALAS DE OPERACIONES, POR SI MUERE UN PACIENTE Y PUEDES VER CÓMO COSECHAN SUS ÓRGANOS.

applications.explanationEn: Te attaches to the unchanged verb vestir and marks one familiar listener as the person dressing.
Para introduces the purpose, while colar stays in its dictionary form inside colarte.
Te attaches to colar in one written word and identifies the familiar listener as the person entering.
Colarte contains the matching te marker, and en introduces the place entered secretly.
Por si introduces the contingency, and muere remains an ordinary present-time form even though the event is only possible.
Puedes changes for one familiar listener, and ver stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Cómo introduces the unknown manner inside a larger statement, so it keeps its written accent without forming a separate direct question.
Espera is a positive command addressed to one familiar listener.

regions.labelEs: O ROBAR SEÑALES DE DESVÍO PARA DIRIGIR EL TRÁFICO DE LA AUTOPISTA HACIA CARRETERAS DE MALA MUERTE PLAGADAS DE ABROJOS. CUANDO REVIENTAN LOS NEUMÁTICOS, EMPIEZAS A DISPARARLE A SUS VENTANAS.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the purpose, and dirigir remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
The three words form the fixed description de mala muerte; mala does not change to match the plural noun before it.
Plagadas has the feminine plural ending that matches carreteras, de introduces what covers them, and abrojos names that material.
Empiezas changes for one familiar listener, a links it to the action, and disparar remains in its dictionary form inside dispararle.
Singular le is attached directly to the unchanged verb disparar in one written word.
The attached le is singular, while the following sus ventanas names a plural target; standard number agreement would normally use les here. The archive's printed form is preserved.

regions.labelEs: LUEGO, CUANDO HUYEN DE SUS COCHES ATERRORIZADOS, LES DAS CAZA A CABALLO, COMO SOLÍAN HACER LOS HOMBRES.

applications.explanationEn: Les marks several targets, das is the form of dar for one familiar listener, and caza completes the fixed pursuit expression.
A and the singular noun caballo form the fixed manner expression without an article.
Solían supplies the past habitual form for several people, and hacer remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Solían uses the imperfect because it presents a customary past behavior rather than one completed event.

regions.labelEs: HACE UN RATO QUE ME DI CUENTA DE QUE ESTAMOS MANTENIENDO CONVERSACIONES COMPLETAMENTE DISTINTAS.

applications.explanationEn: Hace comes before un rato to place the later realization a short while in the past.
Here que connects the elapsed-time phrase to the event it dates; natural English usually restructures the wording rather than translating que alone.
Me matches the speaker, di supplies the completed-past form of dar, cuenta completes the expression, and de que introduces the fact noticed.
Di uses the preterite because it presents the realization as one completed event in the past.
Estamos matches we, and manteniendo supplies the ongoing action with its -iendo ending.
Manteniendo is the ongoing form of mantener, and conversaciones is the plural exchange being carried on.
Completa takes -mente to form completamente, which intensifies how different the conversations are.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.promptEs: darse cuenta de (que) + hecho o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone realizes or becomes aware of something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun, a form of dar, cuenta, and then de before what is realized.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun and dar must match the person: me doy cuenta, te das cuenta, se da cuenta, nos damos cuenta, and so on. Use de before a noun and de que before a full statement. Cuenta is not translated separately in this expression.

example.es: Nos dimos cuenta de que faltaba una llave.
example.en: We realized that a key was missing.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.answerEn: realized; noticed (as part of me he dado cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Dado is the completed-action form of dar, normally ‘given.’ Inside darse cuenta, the whole expression means ‘to realize’ or ‘to notice,’ so dado is not translated as ‘given.’

example.es: Me he dado cuenta del error.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cards.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: I root for; I cheer on
cards.noteEn: Animo is the present form of animar for the speaker. It has no written accent; ánimo with an accent is a noun or an encouraging exclamation.

example.es: Animo a mi equipo desde casa.
example.en: I cheer on my team from home.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Noticias is grammatically plural in Spanish even when English uses the singular mass noun news.

example.es: Veo las noticias por la mañana.
example.en: I watch the news in the morning.

cards.answerEn: of; no separate word before a hoped-for event
cards.noteEn: Esperanza normally uses de before a noun and de que before a full statement about what is hoped for.

example.es: Tengo la esperanza de que vuelva.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps hacerse mean ‘to become’
cards.noteEn: With a describing word, hacerse can present a gradual or noticeable change in the subject's state.

example.es: Los días se hacen más largos.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that a person or thing becomes or gradually grows a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by the word that describes the new state.
cards.noteEn: The short marker and hacer form change with the subject: me hago, te haces, se hace, nos hacemos, and so on. The describing word matches the person or thing in number and, when its form changes, gender.

example.es: Las tardes se hacen más cortas.

cards.answerEn: they will become (as part of se harán)
cards.noteEn: Harán is hacer's future form for more than one subject. With se and a description, hacerse means to become; hacer uses the irregular future stem har-.

example.es: Los días se harán más largos.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.answerEn: they will devastate; they will sweep through
cards.noteEn: Arrasar can mean destroying or devastating a place as something moves through it.

example.en: The flames will devastate the forest.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.
Afectan is the present form used with a plural subject.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en realidad (“actually”)

cards.noteEn: Use it to correct or qualify what someone may believe. It does not mean “currently”; Spanish normally uses actualmente for that meaning.
cards.questionEn: What expression means “actually” or “in fact” when correcting an impression?

example.es: Pensaba que era lunes, pero en realidad es martes.
example.en: I thought it was Monday, but it is actually Tuesday.

cards.answerEn: actually; in fact (as part of en realidad)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone feels bad, unwell, or guilty?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker with a form of sentir, followed by mal.
cards.noteEn: The short marker and sentir change with the person: me siento, te sientes, se siente, and nos sentimos. Mal stays unchanged and can describe physical illness or an unpleasant or guilty feeling.

example.es: Ana se siente mal por el comentario.
example.en: Ana feels bad about the comment.

cards.noteEn: Siento is the form of sentir used by the speaker. With me before it, me siento describes how the speaker feels or what the speaker feels like; this is different from lo siento, the fixed expression for “I'm sorry.”
After sentirse, mal can describe feeling physically unwell or emotionally bad about something.

example.es: Me siento mal por el error.
example.en: I feel bad about the mistake.

cards.noteEn: Na is a very informal dismissive response. Nah is another common spelling; this comic prints na.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is nothing but, or only, a particular thing?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a form of ser, then más que and the thing or description that remains.
cards.noteEn: Ser means “to be” and changes for time and subject: no es más que, no era más que, no fue más que. Más que normally introduces a comparison, but inside this negative frame it restricts the subject to only what follows.

example.es: La llamada no fue más que una broma.
example.en: The call was nothing but a joke.

cards.answerEn: no more than; only (as part of no ser más que)
cards.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” Between a negative form of ser and que, it helps restrict something to the description that follows.

example.es: No fue más que un error.
example.en: It was nothing more than a mistake.

cards.answerEn: than; no separate word in the full expression “nothing but”
cards.noteEn: In no ser más que, que completes the restriction introduced by más. The form of ser changes for the person and time.

example.es: Eso no es más que una idea.
example.en: That is nothing but an idea.

cards.noteEn: Natural has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.
Spanish commonly uses por after atracción or sentir atracción to introduce the object of attraction, where English often uses to.

example.en: She feels an attraction to the sea.

cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.
A transbordador transports people or cargo between points; transbordador espacial is a space shuttle.

example.es: El transbordador lleva pasajeros a la isla.
example.en: The shuttle carries passengers to the island.

cards.noteEn: Espacial can also mean spatial in other contexts. After transbordador, it identifies a space shuttle.
Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “you” verb used with te
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs use te when the person affected is the informal listener. The meaning belongs to the whole verb pattern, so English may not translate te separately.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone misses an event, opportunity, or part of an experience?
cards.answerEn: Use perder with a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker, followed by the thing missed.
cards.noteEn: The marker changes with the person: me pierdo, te pierdes, se pierde, nos perdemos. Here perderse does not mean becoming geographically lost; it means failing to experience something.

example.en: I don't want to miss the concert.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone wants to do?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of querer, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Querer changes to match the person and time, while the desired action stays unchanged: quiero salir, quieres comer, queremos dormir. Spanish does not insert a between the two verbs.

cards.answerEn: to miss; to miss out on
cards.noteEn: With a matching me, te, or se marker, perderse algo means failing to experience an event or opportunity. With two verbs, that marker may appear before the first conjugated verb: no te quieres perder.

example.en: I don't want to miss the movie.

cards.noteEn: Vestirte joins the unchanged verb vestir, to dress, with te, which identifies one familiar listener as the person being dressed.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: as (in the role or capacity of)
cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the role, identity, or point of view from which someone speaks or acts. This is different from cómo with an accent, which asks “how.”

example.en: As a doctor, I recommend resting.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Colarte joins colar with te. In the pronominal verb colarse, it means entering somewhere secretly or without permission.

example.es: No debes colarte en la fiesta.
example.en: You should not sneak into the party.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone sneaks into a place?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker with a form of colar, then en and the place.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form is colarse. In present-time forms, its o often changes to ue: ella se cuela. En introduces the place entered secretly or without permission.

example.es: Ella se cuela en la fiesta.

cards.answerEn: into; required after colarse before a place
cards.noteEn: Use en after colarse to introduce the place entered secretly.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
A sala de operaciones is an operating room used for surgery.

example.es: El hospital tiene dos salas de operaciones.
example.en: The hospital has two operating rooms.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por si, 'in case'
cards.noteEn: Por combines with unaccented si before a possible event to form por si.

example.es: Lleva agua por si hace calor.
example.en: Take water in case it is hot.

cards.questionEn: How do you say 'in case' before a possible event?
cards.answerEn: Use por si, then an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: Si has no accent here. Even when the possible event lies in the future, Spanish normally uses a present-time form after por si: por si llueve, not a future form. The main clause names the precaution.

example.es: Lleva un abrigo por si hace frío.
example.en: Take a coat in case it is cold.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por si, 'in case'
cards.noteEn: Si remains unaccented in por si and introduces the uncertain event for which someone prepares.

example.es: Cierra la ventana por si llueve.
example.en: Close the window in case it rains.

cards.noteEn: Paciente has the same written form for a male or female patient.

example.en: The patient is waiting for the doctor.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.questionEn: When “what,” “how,” or “where” introduces unknown information inside a larger sentence, does Spanish keep the written accent?
cards.answerEn: Yes. Keep the accent in qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuál, or quién even when the question is embedded inside a statement.
cards.noteEn: An embedded, or indirect, question reports what is unknown rather than asking it as a separate sentence. It may have no question marks, but the question word still carries its accent. Compare no sé dónde vive, “I don't know where she lives,” with the relative form donde in la casa donde vive, “the house where she lives.”

example.en: I don't know where she lives.

cards.noteEn: Cosechar literally means gathering a crop and can extend to harvesting organs in medical language.

example.en: They harvest the grapes in September.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
Señal can be a physical sign that directs road users, not only a signal or indication.
Dirigir can mean sending movement or traffic toward a destination.

example.es: Van a dirigir el tráfico hacia el puente.
example.en: They are going to direct traffic toward the bridge.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de mala muerte
cards.noteEn: De is fixed inside de mala muerte, a description meaning seedy, shabby, or disreputable.

example.es: Entraron en un bar de mala muerte.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe a place or thing as seedy, shabby, or disreputable?
cards.answerEn: Put de mala muerte after the noun.
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed description, not a literal reference to death. Its wording stays de mala muerte even after a masculine or plural noun.

example.es: Dormimos en un hotel de mala muerte.
example.en: We slept in a seedy hotel.

cards.noteEn: Mala is part of the fixed expression de mala muerte rather than an ordinary adjective agreeing with the preceding noun.

example.es: Es un hotel de mala muerte.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes de mala muerte
cards.noteEn: The full expression de mala muerte describes something as shabby or disreputable; it is not a literal reference to death.

example.es: Trabaja en un local de mala muerte.
example.en: He works in a shabby establishment.

cards.noteEn: Plagadas agrees with a feminine plural noun and is followed by de before what fills or overruns it.

example.es: Las calles están plagadas de baches.
example.en: The streets are riddled with potholes.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is riddled with or overrun by something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of plagado that matches the described noun, then de and what fills it.
cards.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as informe or calles. Plagado changes to plagada, plagados, or plagadas to match that noun; de stays unchanged before what is present in an unwanted abundance.

example.es: El informe está plagado de errores.
example.en: The report is riddled with errors.

cards.noteEn: Plagado de introduces what something is filled, covered, or overrun with.

example.es: El texto está plagado de errores.
example.en: The text is riddled with errors.

cards.noteEn: Abrojo can also name a thorny burr. On a road here, the plural refers to sharp obstacles placed to puncture tires.
Reventar describes something bursting; with tires, English commonly says blow out.

example.es: Los globos revientan con el calor.
example.en: The balloons burst in the heat.

cards.noteEn: Empiezas is empezar's present form for one familiar listener.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone starts doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of empezar, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Empezar changes for the person and time; a stays fixed, and the action verb stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)
to shoot at him, her, or it
cards.noteEn: Dispararle joins disparar with singular le, which marks one target. Use dispararles when that target is plural; a following phrase beginning with a can name the target explicitly.

example.en: You must not shoot at the animal.

cards.answerEn: at; introduces the target after disparar
cards.noteEn: After disparar, a can introduce the person or thing aimed at.
Huyen is huir's present form for a plural subject.

example.en: The animals flee from the fire.

cards.noteEn: Coche commonly means “car” in Spain. Other Spanish-speaking regions may prefer carro or auto.

example.es: Hay muchos coches en la calle.
example.en: There are many cars in the street.

cards.answerEn: them; marks several targets of dar caza
cards.noteEn: In dar caza a alguien, le or les can stand before dar for the person or people being pursued.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone hunts down or pursues a target?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dar followed by caza, then a and the target; a target already known can instead be represented by le or les before dar.
cards.noteEn: Only dar changes for the person and time: doy caza, das caza, dan caza. Caza stays fixed. Al is the required combination of a and el, as in dar caza al fugitivo; le is singular and les is plural when those short target words are used.

example.es: La policía da caza al fugitivo.
example.en: The police hunt down the fugitive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; supplies the verb in dar caza, 'to hunt down'
cards.noteEn: Das is dar's present form for one familiar listener. In dar caza, dar is not translated literally as give.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes dar caza, 'to hunt down'
cards.noteEn: Caza means hunting by itself, but dar caza works as a fixed expression for pursuing and catching a target.

example.es: La policía da caza al ladrón.
example.en: The police hunt down the thief.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a caballo, 'on horseback'
cards.noteEn: The fixed expression uses a before caballo without an article.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone travels or does something on horseback?
cards.answerEn: Use a caballo after the action.
cards.noteEn: A caballo is a fixed manner expression. The a has no separate English word here, caballo stays singular, and Spanish does not put an article between them.

cards.answerEn: they used to; they would usually
cards.noteEn: Solían is soler's imperfect-past form for more than one person. It is followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of soler followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Soler adds the idea of a habit. Suelo means “I usually,” while solía means “I used to.” The action after it stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form: suelo caminar, solía caminar.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone usually does something, or used to do it?

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.

cards.answerEn: one; a certain (before a masculine time word)
cards.noteEn: Before a masculine time word, un can point to one unspecified occasion rather than simply serving as the article “a.”

example.en: One day I will return to Granada.

cards.answerEn: while; a short or unspecified period of time
cards.noteEn: Un rato refers to an imprecise stretch of time. Its length depends on the situation rather than on a fixed number of minutes.

cards.answerEn: since; no separate English word in a natural ‘a while ago’ translation
cards.noteEn: After hace and an amount of elapsed time, que can connect that time to the event being dated. English often restructures the idea rather than translating que by itself.

example.es: Hace un mes que hablé con Ana.
example.en: I spoke with Ana a month ago.

cards.answerEn: realized; noticed (as part of me di cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Di is dar's completed-past form for the speaker. With me and cuenta, it forms me di cuenta, not the literal meaning gave.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Manteniendo is mantener's ongoing-action form. With conversación, mantener can mean having, carrying on, or keeping a conversation going rather than physically maintaining something.

example.en: We are having a calm conversation.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that people have or carry on a conversation?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of mantener with conversación, or conversaciones for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Mantener literally often means to keep or maintain, but with conversación it describes having or carrying on the exchange. Mantener changes with the person and time; for example, yo mantengo and estamos manteniendo.
